prompt: Your school wants to improve biodiversity on campus. Write a text for school leaders in which you explain current problems, recommend realistic actions, and describe how students could measure whether the project is helping local wildlife.
requirements: Recommend realistic habitat or management actions.
Describe how students could measure outcomes over time.
purpose: Recommend a measurable school biodiversity project
textTypeRationale: A proposal suits a decision-making task requiring problems, recommendations, implementation and evaluation.
modelAnswerJa: Tree plantingだけに頼らず、native plants・mowing・lighting・monitoringを組み合わせています。生徒がdataを集めてimpactを評価する点がtask fulfillmentを強めています。
modelAnswer:
Proposal: Building a More Biodiverse School Campus

Aim

This proposal recommends a practical biodiversity programme that turns selected parts of the school grounds into better habitat for insects, birds and other local species while creating opportunities for student learning.

Current issues

Most of the campus is designed for neatness and convenience. Large areas of short grass provide limited food or shelter for wildlife, ornamental plants are replaced frequently, and outdoor lighting remains bright late into the evening. None of these choices is individually disastrous, but together they create a landscape with little variety.

Recommended actions

1. Replace selected lawn areas with native planting

The school should convert small areas that are not needed for sport or movement into native flower and grass beds. Native plants are more likely to support local insects and generally require less intensive maintenance once established.

This should begin as a trial rather than a complete redesign. Two or three visible areas would allow the school to test maintenance needs and student response.

2. Change mowing practices

Not every grass area needs to be cut at the same frequency. Allowing some edges and unused zones to grow longer can create habitat at almost no additional cost. Clear paths and regularly cut borders would keep the site looking intentional rather than neglected.

3. Improve shelter and water

Bird boxes, insect nesting structures and shallow water sources can help, but they should be placed according to expert guidance. Decorative bug hotels are not useful if they are poorly designed or located where they become too hot or wet.

4. Review lighting

Facilities staff should identify outdoor lights that remain on unnecessarily after school activities finish. Shielding lights and using timers could reduce disturbance to nocturnal wildlife while also saving energy.

Student participation

The project should become part of science and environmental learning. Students could complete simple species counts at the same locations several times each year. Photographs, insect observations and bird records could be stored in a shared database.

Measurement

Success should not be judged by whether the campus merely looks greener. The school should compare:
• the number and variety of species observed;
• flowering periods and pollinator visits;
• maintenance time and water use;
• student participation in monitoring.

Baseline observations should be collected before major changes are made.

Costs and maintenance

The programme should use gradual changes so that costs remain manageable. Some funds currently spent on frequent mowing or replacing ornamental plants could be redirected toward native planting. Local conservation groups may also be willing to advise students.

Conclusion

A school cannot recreate a complete natural ecosystem inside its grounds, but it can stop treating every outdoor space as decoration. By increasing plant diversity, reducing unnecessary disturbance and collecting evidence, our campus could support more wildlife and become a living classroom at the same time.

The strongest project would not simply plant more. It would observe, learn and adapt.

prompt: Your school is holding an assembly about the environmental and social impacts of fast fashion. Write a text in which you explain why cheap clothing can have hidden costs, suggest realistic changes for students, and persuade the audience to avoid both overconsumption and unrealistic perfection.
requirements: Explain environmental and social hidden costs of fast fashion.
Suggest realistic actions students can take.
Persuade the audience to improve habits without demanding perfect consumption.
textTypeRationale: A speech allows direct engagement with students and can combine information with a realistic call to action.
modelAnswerJa: 『買わないことが正義』という極端な主張を避け、buy less / wear longer / repair / second-handなど現実的な行動を提示しています。Speechらしい直接的な呼びかけを使っています。
modelAnswer:
Good morning everyone,

Think about the cheapest item of clothing you bought this year. Maybe it cost less than lunch. Cheap clothing can feel like a bargain, especially when trends change quickly and social media constantly shows us new outfits. But a low price at the checkout does not mean the real cost is low.

Fast fashion depends on producing large quantities of clothing quickly and selling them at prices that encourage frequent replacement. The environmental cost begins with materials. Cotton can require large amounts of water, while synthetic fabrics are usually made from fossil fuels and can release tiny plastic fibres during washing. Dyeing, manufacturing and transport also use energy and create pollution.

There is a human cost as well. Clothing supply chains are complex, and low prices can place pressure on factories to reduce labour costs. Not every inexpensive item is produced in an abusive workplace, and an expensive label is not automatically ethical. Still, extremely low prices should make us ask how workers are being paid and protected.

So should we all stop buying new clothes? That sounds simple, but it is not realistic for everyone. People grow, uniforms wear out, bodies change and families have different budgets. Environmental responsibility should not become another way to judge people for what they can afford.

A better goal is to reduce unnecessary consumption.

First, wear clothes for longer. The most sustainable item is often the one already in your wardrobe. Before buying something new for one event, ask whether you can borrow, swap or combine clothes differently.

Second, learn basic repair. Sewing on a button or fixing a small tear can extend the life of an item dramatically. Our school could run a repair workshop or clothing-swap day once each term.

Third, use second-hand options when they work for you. Buying used clothing does not solve every problem, but it can reduce demand for new production and make higher-quality items more affordable.

Fourth, when you do buy new, slow down. Ask whether you will wear the item many times, whether the quality is reasonable and whether the company provides useful information about its supply chain. Do not assume every green label is meaningful; vague marketing is not evidence.

Finally, resist the pressure to treat clothing as disposable content. An outfit does not become useless because it has appeared in a photograph before.

None of us will make perfect choices. Perfection is a poor environmental strategy because it makes people give up when they cannot meet an impossible standard. Progress is more useful: buy less often, choose more carefully, care for what you own and keep useful clothing in circulation.

Fashion can still be creative and enjoyable. The challenge is to express ourselves without acting as if every new trend requires a new purchase.

Thank you.

prompt: After a long drought, your city is introducing temporary household water restrictions. Write a text for a local newspaper in which you explain why restrictions may be necessary, address concerns about fairness, and recommend how the city should reduce water use while protecting vulnerable residents.
requirements: Explain why temporary restrictions may be necessary.
Address fairness concerns between households, businesses and vulnerable residents.
Recommend practical measures beyond simply asking everyone to use less water.
purpose: Support fair and practical drought measures
textTypeRationale: A letter to the editor fits a community debate and allows the writer to support action while questioning how it is designed.
modelAnswerJa: Restrictionsを支持しながら、householdsだけに責任を負わせないfairnessの視点を入れています。Short-term emergency measuresとlong-term infrastructureの両方を扱っています。
modelAnswer:
Dear Editor,

After months of unusually low rainfall, the city has announced temporary restrictions on household water use. Predictably, some residents have called the measures unnecessary, while others want even stricter limits. The real question should not be whether restrictions are pleasant. They are not. The question is whether they are necessary, fair and part of a wider plan.

During a serious drought, voluntary requests may not reduce demand quickly enough. Reservoirs and groundwater systems need time to recover, and essential services such as hospitals, sanitation and firefighting require reliable supplies. Temporary limits on activities such as watering large lawns or repeatedly washing cars can therefore be reasonable.

However, fairness matters. A rule that tells every household to reduce use by the same percentage can affect people differently. A family of six cannot use the same amount of water as one person living alone. People with certain medical needs may require additional water, and renters may have little control over leaking plumbing or inefficient appliances.

The city should therefore combine restrictions with targeted support. Basic household use should remain protected, while high-volume non-essential use can face stronger limits. Residents with documented medical or accessibility needs should have a simple exemption process that does not require repeated applications.

Businesses also need clear rules. Restaurants, farms, construction companies and factories use water in different ways, so the city should publish sector-specific expectations rather than focusing public attention entirely on households. Large users should report conservation measures and, where practical, adopt recycling or more efficient equipment.

Enforcement should begin with information, not punishment. Many people waste water because they do not realize a pipe is leaking or because they do not know which activities use the most. The city could offer free or subsidized leak checks for low-income households and provide rebates for efficient fixtures.

Long-term planning is equally important. Emergency restrictions cannot become a substitute for repairing ageing pipes, improving water storage and preparing for more variable rainfall. If residents are asked to make sacrifices while the public system loses large quantities through leaks, trust will disappear quickly.

The city should also publish weekly data showing reservoir levels, total demand and progress toward conservation targets. People are more likely to cooperate when they can see why restrictions exist and whether they are working.

Drought policy should protect essential needs first, reduce waste second and share responsibility fairly. Residents must change some habits, but households should not carry the whole burden.

Temporary restrictions can be justified when water supplies are genuinely threatened. They will be far more effective if the city combines them with transparent data, targeted assistance, business responsibility and serious investment in the system that delivers the water in the first place.

Yours faithfully,

A concerned resident
